conventions.convention: A feedforward graph is finite and acyclic, carries a specified topological ordering, and evaluates each non-input vertex by a scalar activation of an affine combination. Layered MLPs use a shared hidden activation and identity output activation.
Single-hidden-layer networks have arbitrary real input weights, hidden biases, output weights, and an output bias. Width zero is allowed and realizes constants.

Countable Choice is assumed for the Lebesgue convention. M consists of real-valued Lebesgue-measurable, locally essentially bounded activations whose discontinuity-set closure is null. M_pt additionally requires pointwise local boundedness. Polynomial almost everywhere means equality to one real polynomial outside a Lebesgue-null set.
Test functions are complex-valued and distributions complex-linear. A real distribution takes real values on real-valued tests; the polynomial conclusion is for real distributions.

The Lp equivalence uses 1<p<∞ and a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact set, absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Raw networks represent classes through Borel representatives equal Lebesgue-almost everywhere. Necessity requires positive total mass; the zero measure is treated separately.
Pointwise compact-uniform approximation uses M_pt. The broader M conclusion uses d-dimensional Lebesgue essential supremum on K, which is identically zero when K is Lebesgue null.
Polynomial ridge degree k ranges over nonnegative integers, with s^0=1 for every real s, including zero.

load_bearing.statement: Uniform clause: Assume Countable Choice and fix d≥1. For every compact K⊆R^d, if σ∈M_pt is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family with arbitrary affine hidden inputs and output bias is uniformly dense in C(K,R).

Assume Countable Choice. Let d≥1, let K⊆R^d be compact, and let σ∈M_pt not agree almost everywhere with any polynomial. Then the finite scalar single-hidden-layer networks with activation σ are uniformly dense in C(K,R).

Assume Countable Choice. Let σ∈M. If every convolution with a smooth test function supported in [-1,1] is a polynomial, then σ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial. Equivalently, if σ is not polynomial almost everywhere, at least one such test function has a nonpolynomial convolution.

Assume Countable Choice. Let σ∈M_pt, φ∈C_c^∞(R;C), and K⊆R compact. For g=σ*φ, Re g and Im g are each uniform limits on K of finite real linear combinations of translates of σ with an optional constant.

Let g:R→R be infinitely differentiable and not a polynomial. For every d≥1 and compact K⊆R^d, scalar networks with one hidden layer, activation g, arbitrary affine hidden inputs and linear output are uniformly dense in C(K,R).
Assume Countable Choice. Let d≥1, w∈R^d be nonzero, b∈R, and E⊆R have Lebesgue outer measure zero. Then {x:w·x+b∈E} is Lebesgue measurable and has d-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let σ∈M. If every convolution of σ with a real smooth test function supported in [-1,1] is a real polynomial, then one nonnegative integer N bounds the degrees of all these convolutions.
For every nondegenerate compact interval I=[a,b], the real smooth functions on R vanishing outside I are separable for the displayed metric generated by uniform bounds on all derivatives.

Assume Countable Choice. Let d≥1, q≥0, and let measurable σ equal almost everywhere a polynomial of degree at most q, including zero. No finite single-hidden-layer σ-network approximates f(te₁)=t^(q+1) on 0≤t≤1 uniformly with error less than (q+1)!/[2^(q+2)(q+1)^(q+1)].
Assume Countable Choice. For every integer d≥1, the zero set of a nonzero real polynomial in d variables is Lebesgue measurable and has d-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

Let μ be a finite regular Borel measure on R^d concentrated on compact K, and let 1≤p<∞. Using the Borel sigma-algebra, restrictions to K of real compactly supported continuous functions on R^d are dense in real Lp(μ).

concerns.concern: The Given formula uses “t=1/n for some n∈N”, and step 1.1 repeats the spike set {1/n:n∈N}, without excluding zero. The published def-natural-numbers defines N=ω with 0∈N, so these expressions include the undefined reciprocal 1/0. Specify positive integers for the spike indices. The subsequent argument works with n≥1.

seams_checked.note: def-relu-network specializes the finite acyclic graph convention and explicitly supplies its additional edge, depth, and complexity conventions.
The transformer definitions use finite positionwise feedforward maps. Their separate attention and expressivity assumptions do not invoke the single-hidden-layer theorem with stronger conclusions.

The neural-operator definitions use finite MLPs. The universality theorem's F6 and step 1.2 use only compact-uniform ReLU approximation under Countable Choice; vector approximation follows by stacking finitely many scalar approximants.

This is a contextual page prerequisite. The recurrence algorithm and gradient theorem use their own finite-program and C1 hypotheses, with no stronger universality or activation-differentiability inference.
The initialization procedure and variance results use the finite layered affine-sum architecture; probability assumptions and zero-at-kink conventions are stated independently.
The particle-measure definition reproduces finite ridge sums using atoms with scaled output coefficients, treats width zero separately, and adds the optional output bias separately.
def-spectral-network-complexity explicitly identifies the supplier as broader architectural context and independently defines its vector activations and zero-bias recurrence.
This is a contextual page prerequisite. The finite-description result assumes measurable score maps and a compressor; it does not infer compression or generalization from approximation universality.
The encoder/decoder definitions and procedure use finite graph evaluation as architectural notation and state measurability and gradient requirements separately.
The contrastive-loss definition presents finite feedforward networks as one possible encoder realization and makes no universality-to-alignment inference.
The linear-layer definition correctly specializes to identity output activation and zero bias; its matrix dimensions and factorization conventions are supplied independently.
